analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income tax rates with a single 17% flat tax and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The 17% flat-tax bill drew zero cosponsors, never got a committee hearing or floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would scrap the entire progressive income tax — with its higher rates on higher incomes — and replace it with one 17% rate. It taxes only wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits at the individual level, leaving investment income like capital gains and dividends outside a business untaxed. It repeals the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, and every income tax credit, including the earned income and child tax credits. It would also loosen pension rules so employers could pull money out of overfunded pension plans and rewrite a constitutional-style rule making future tax increases much harder to pass.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: a top marginal rate of 37% becomes 17%, the estate tax disappears, and capital gains and dividends held outside a business face no individual tax at all. Large corporations and pass-through businesses see the 21% corporate rate drop to 17% and a simpler business tax. Employers with overfunded pension plans gain the right to reclaim excess pension assets, paying only the 17% tax instead of a heavy excise tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and employers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a single 17% rate on individual taxable income, replacing the graduated rates that climb to 37% [S2][S3].

Taxes individuals only on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, so investment income such as capital gains, dividends, and interest held outside a business activity is not taxed at the individual level [S3].
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2021 [S2][S3].
Repeals the alternative minimum tax and all income tax credits, and replaces the corporate income tax with a 17% tax on all business income regardless of business form [S2][S3].

Repeals pension nondiscrimination, contribution limit, and distribution rules, and lets employers transfer excess pension assets to themselves with the amount taxed only as income, repealing the excise tax on such reversions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Low- and moderate-income working families who rely on tax credits like the earned income tax credit and the child tax credit lose them outright, with only a larger standard deduction in return. Households whose wealth comes from investments keep that income largely untaxed while wage earners pay 17% from the first dollar above the deduction. Federal revenue would fall substantially, forcing either spending cuts, larger deficits, or both.

drawbacks.text: Repealing all income tax credits eliminates the earned income tax credit and child tax credit, which currently reduce or erase tax bills for millions of low-wage working families; a flat deduction does not fully replace them [S2][S3].

Repealing pension nondiscrimination and minimum participation rules would allow retirement plans that favor executives over rank-and-file workers, and allowing employer reversions of excess pension assets with only income inclusion shifts money from worker pension plans back to company balance sheets [S3].

The bill bars Congress from considering any bill that raises a tax rate, creates a rate, cuts the standard deduction, or reduces revenue, unless three-fifths of each chamber votes to waive the ban — locking in whatever distribution of taxes it creates and making future tax policy changes far harder [S3].
A large revenue loss would require offsetting federal spending cuts or higher deficits, with the burden of any cuts falling on the programs and services ordinary people use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Simplification is real: one rate and a big standard deduction would genuinely cut compliance burdens for many middle-income wage earners, and the deduction amounts are large enough that lower-income filers would owe little or nothing on wages. But the distribution tips sharply toward the top — the top rate falls from 37% to 17%, the estate tax disappears entirely, and investment income escapes individual taxation — while low-income families lose refundable credits worth more to them than the deduction they gain. Pension rule repeals tilt retirement plans toward executives. On balance, the gains concentrate at the top and the costs concentrate further down the income scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 17, 2021, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the SMART Act in the Senate on May 17, 2021 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without a committee markup, a floor vote, or any companion House action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained; the tax code stayed exactly as it was. In practical terms, high-income households and large estates avoided the rate cuts and estate tax repeal this bill would have delivered, and working families kept the tax credits it would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax code — no one changed

for.what_they_did: Introduced the SMART Act on May 17, 2021 and made no visible effort to build cosponsor support; the bill drew none [S1][S4][S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 17, 2021 and never held a markup, hearing on the bill, or advanced it to the floor [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors joined from either party and no vote ever occurred, so there was no observable partisan alignment — a flat-tax bill introduced by a single retiring Republican senator with zero support.

industries.industry: High-income households and the wealthiest estates
industries.note: A single 17% rate replaces rates up to 37%, the estate and gift taxes are repealed, and investment income outside a business goes untaxed at the individual level. The bill's gains flow overwhelmingly to the top of the income and wealth distribution.

industries.industry: Employers with overfunded defined-benefit pension plans
industries.note: The bill repeals the excise tax on employer reversions and lets companies pull excess pension assets back into the business, paying only 17% as income. Assets that back worker pension promises become company money.

The 21% corporate rate drops to 17% and the same rate applies uniformly to partnerships and sole proprietorships, with a simpler tax base. Some pass-through owners would owe the 17% business tax on income currently taxed at individual rates that can be lower for smaller businesses, so the effect varies by firm size and income.

industries.industry: Low-wage working families claiming refundable credits
industries.note: Repeal of all income tax credits eliminates the earned income tax credit and child tax credit. The bill's larger per-dependent standard deduction does not replace the cash benefit these credits provide to families with little or no tax liability.

industries.industry: State and local governments and tax-exempt organizations
industries.note: The bill imposes a 17% employer tax on the value of noncash (excludable) compensation — health benefits, fringe benefits — provided by tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local government employers, a new direct cost on public and nonprofit employers.

Repeal of nondiscrimination testing, contribution limits, and distribution restrictions removes much of the compliance apparatus the industry administers and relaxes limits on high earners' contributions, but the pension simplification landscape would also be rewritten wholesale.
